metaTitle: FICO Score vs VantageScore for Loans and Free Apps
metaDescription: FICO Score vs VantageScore use the same 300 to 850 range but different formulas. See why your two scores differ and how to find the one your lender pulls.
h1: FICO Score vs VantageScore on the Same Credit Report
subtitle: A side-by-side look at the two best-known credit scoring brands and why the score on a free app may not match the one a lender pulls.
introText:
[FICO Score](https://www.fico.com/en/products/fico-score) and [VantageScore](https://www.vantagescore.com) are two competing credit scoring models that both read your credit report and both generally run from 300 to 850. The practical difference in FICO Score vs VantageScore is which model a given lender pulls and how each one handles a thin or recent credit file. At ModernWallet, we publish free calculators and plain-language money guides, and every credit guide we write starts from the score the lender will read.

The [Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB)](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-is-a-fico-score-en-315/) states that you do not have just one credit score. A score can differ by scoring model, by data source, and even by the day it was calculated. Two different numbers on two screens can both be legitimate readings of the same credit history.

sections.heading: Two Models, One Credit Report
sections.content:
FICO and VantageScore are two scoring brands that run the same kind of credit report data through different formulas. The CFPB describes a credit score as a prediction of your credit behavior, such as how likely you are to pay a loan back on time. Companies build that prediction with a scoring model, which is a mathematical formula applied to the information in your credit report.

The data both models read comes from the credit bureaus. Both brands use the 300 to 850 range in their widely used versions, and the CFPB notes that most credit scores fall in that range. Because the scales match, a FICO number and a VantageScore number look interchangeable on a screen, even though separate formulas produced them.

Lenders choose which model and which version they use. Many mortgage, auto, and credit card lenders use a FICO version, and some free credit monitoring services show VantageScore. For any single application, the score that counts is the one that lender pulls, so ask the lender which model and version it uses.

Each model also has its own way of scoring a thin or recent credit file, meaning a report with little history on it. We do not quote a minimum credit history for either one. If your file is thin, read our comparison of [secured vs unsecured credit cards](/compare/secured-credit-card-vs-unsecured-credit-card/) and our list of the [best secured credit cards](/roundup/best-secured-credit-cards/) before you apply for a first card.

sections.heading: Why Your Two Scores Do Not Match
sections.content:
Your FICO Score and VantageScore will not match because of three causes the CFPB names: the scoring model, the data source, and the day the score was calculated. Each cause can move the number on its own. Together they explain why an app and a lender can show different figures in the same week.

The scoring model is the first cause. FICO and VantageScore weigh your report with different formulas, and the CFPB adds that the model used can depend on the type of loan product the score is for. A lender scoring an auto loan and a free app scoring your file for general monitoring may be running different formulas.

The data source is the second cause. Both models read credit report data from the credit bureaus, and a score built from one data source starts from different inputs than a score built from another. When two scores come from different sources, part of the gap exists in the data before any formula runs.

The calculation date is the third cause. A score can differ depending on the day it was calculated. Compare scores calculated close together if you want to isolate the model difference.

A gap between the two numbers does not mean either score is wrong. Both models compute from the same kind of credit report data, so the scores usually move in the same direction when your habits change. A rising VantageScore and a rising FICO Score point to the same improvement, even when the two numbers never line up.

sections.heading: What Both Scoring Models Weigh
sections.content:
FICO and VantageScore both draw on the factors the CFPB lists as typical inputs to scoring models. Three of those factors describe how you pay: your bill-paying history, your current unpaid debt, and how much of your available credit you are using. Three more describe the shape of your file: the number and type of loan accounts, how long accounts have been open, and new applications for credit.

The last factor on the CFPB list is whether you have had a debt sent to collections, a foreclosure, or a bankruptcy, and how long ago it happened. We do not give a percentage weight for each factor on this page. The useful point for a borrower is direction: a habit that improves these inputs usually lifts both scores together.

Bill-paying history and how much available credit you use are data that FICO and VantageScore both read. According to the CFPB, a higher score usually makes it easier to qualify for a loan and may bring a better interest rate or loan terms. Our guide to the [credit score for a 0% annual percentage rate (APR) credit card](/guides/credit-score-for-0-apr-credit-card/) shows how that works for one card type.

If you plan to move a balance from one card to another, compare offers in our [best balance transfer credit cards](/roundup/best-balance-transfer-credit-cards/) list. If you are still deciding whether to use credit at all, our [credit card vs debit card](/compare/credit-card-vs-debit-card/) comparison covers that choice first.

sections.heading: Accuracy in the FICO Score vs VantageScore Question
sections.content:
We have no independent accuracy comparison of FICO and VantageScore to cite, so we do not name a winner on accuracy. Each model is a prediction of the same thing, your chance of paying back a loan on time, built with its own formula. For a borrower, the useful test is whether the score you watch is the same model and version the lender reads.

A VantageScore still helps when the lender pulls FICO. The two usually move in the same direction when your habits change. That signal is about direction only.

A VantageScore cannot tell you the exact number a FICO-based lender will see. If an offer lists a minimum score, ask the lender which model sets that cutoff before you compare it with any free score. Matching the model first keeps you from applying on the strength of a number the lender never uses.

sections.heading: Which Score to Watch Before You Apply
sections.content:
Watch the score your lender uses, and between applications, watch the trend in one free score from one source. Both models usually move in the same direction when your habits change, while their numbers stay apart.

Pick one free score and stick with it. Note the model name it shows, check it on a regular schedule, and compare each reading with the last reading from the same app. Switching apps breaks the comparison, because a change of model or data source can move the number with no change in your habits.

Do not read the gap between a VantageScore on an app and a FICO Score from a lender as a drop in your credit. That gap comes from the model, the data source, or the calculation date, the three causes the CFPB lists. Your payment habits may be exactly the same as last month.

Before an application, ask the lender two questions: which scoring model and version it uses, and which credit bureau report it pulls. With those answers, you can tell whether your free score comes from the same model as the decision or serves only as a general trend line.

sections.heading: Free Credit Apps and the FICO Score vs VantageScore Gap
sections.content:
The score on a free credit app is a real score from a real scoring model, though it may come from a different model than the one a lender pulls. Some free monitoring services show VantageScore. That means the number on an app and the number behind a loan decision can come from different formulas.

You can get your scores for free through several legitimate channels; see our guide to [what a good credit score is](/guides/what-is-a-good-credit-score/). Before you compare a free score with a lender's number, confirm which model the free score uses. Look for the model name next to the score, and if the app does not show one, treat the number as a general signal until you know its source.

Pull your credit reports this week, write down which model each free score uses, and ask your next lender which score it pulls.

verdict: Watch the FICO Score if a lender confirms it pulls a FICO version for a mortgage, auto loan, or credit card application, because that number drives the decision. Treat a free VantageScore as a trend line between applications. It shows whether your habits are moving your credit in the right direction, even though its number will not match the lender's. This advice does not serve a borrower whose lender says it pulls VantageScore. In that case, watch VantageScore closely and use any FICO number you can get as the trend line instead. It also does not serve someone with a thin or recent file who needs an exact score to clear a lender's cutoff, because each model scores thin files under its own rules. That borrower should ask the lender for the exact score it used and read our secured card comparison before applying for new credit. Our answer would change if a lender told you it uses VantageScore, or if a free service began showing the same model and version your lender pulls, because the free number would then track the decision directly. Before your next application, ask the lender whether it pulls a FICO Score or a VantageScore, and which version.

faqItems.question: What is the difference between FICO and VantageScore?
faqItems.answer: FICO and VantageScore are two competing credit scoring models that read the same kind of credit report data with different formulas. Both use a 300 to 850 range in their widely used versions. The practical difference is which model a lender pulls and how each handles a thin or recent credit file, so the same credit history can produce two different, legitimate numbers.

faqItems.question: Which is more accurate, FICO or VantageScore?
faqItems.answer: We do not name either model as more accurate, because we have no independent accuracy comparison to cite. Each is a prediction of how likely you are to pay a loan back on time. For a loan application, the more useful score is the one the lender pulls, so ask the lender which model and version it uses.

faqItems.question: Why is my VantageScore different from my FICO score?
faqItems.answer: Your VantageScore and FICO Score differ because they come from different scoring models, and the CFPB notes that scores can also differ by data source and by the day they were calculated. Both models read the same kind of credit report data, so they usually move in the same direction when your habits change. The two numbers are not expected to match.

faqItems.question: Do lenders use FICO or VantageScore?
faqItems.answer: Lenders choose which scoring model and which version they use. Many mortgage, auto, and credit card lenders use a FICO version, and some free credit monitoring services show VantageScore. We cannot give a percentage of lenders using each model, so ask the lender which score it pulls before you apply.

faqItems.question: Is the score on my free credit app my real credit score?
faqItems.answer: Yes, a free app shows a real credit score, though it is one of several scores you have. The CFPB states that you do not have just one credit score, and some free services show VantageScore while a lender may pull a FICO version. Confirm which model the app uses before you compare it with a lender's number.
